title: Cambridgeshire trio climb North Africa’s highest peak and raise £9,000 for charity
content: Three friends from Cambridgeshire have scaled the highest peak in North Africa. James Baker, 35, from Ramsey, Paul Mallinson, 65, from Houghton, and Tamar Mullard, 45, from Whittlesey took on Mount Toubkal in Morocco. Their five-day ascent raised more than £9,000 for Sue Ryder’s palliative, end-of-life care, and bereavement support services. Paul, Tamar and James (Image: Sue Ryder ) James said: "There is no doubt that the challenge was hard – in fact by far the hardest thing I have ever done – and exhausting." He said the trek was in memory of his father, Peter, who died from oesophageal cancer at the age of 54. James said: "Even though Dad was only in a hospice for two days, those two days were completely different from his time hospital. The hike (Image: Sue Ryder) "The hospice staff were amazing." Paul said the climb, which totalled 70,000 steps and 34 miles, was tougher than he had anticipated. Paul said: "At 70,000 steps and 34 miles, the climb and descent was longer than I expected, and I had to keep reminding myself why I was doing it." title: Historic barn near Grade I listed Hunts property could become five-bedroom home
content: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans have been submitted to turn a historic outbuilding beside a Grade I listed building into a five-bedroom home. Mick Hilless has applied to Huntingdonshire District Council to turn a barn and office building linked to Bodsey House into a home on Bodsey Toll Road, Ramsey. Bodsey House is Grade I listed, meaning it is of exceptional interest. The property was once a 13th-century hermitage belonging to Ramsey Abbey but has since been altered and turned into a family home. The plans would turn the barn and office building at the rear of the site into one five-bedroom home. The historic barn is curtilage listed, which means it is legally protected as it sits within the grounds of a listed building. Documents by Scroxton Architects say the barn and office building are dilapidated and no longer suitable for modern agricultural or commercial use.
